Original learning chapter · updated 9 September 2026. Equations and examples explain concepts; they are not test acceptance or a support matrix.

Prerequisites: No previous chapter required.

Numbers need a frame

A point describes a location; a vector describes a displacement. “Three units to the right” is incomplete until we say whose right and what a unit means. A mesh can be authored in object coordinates, placed in world coordinates, then expressed relative to a camera. The underlying point does not change just because its coordinates do. Confusing those frames is a common source of mirrored, displaced or incorrectly lit geometry.

A three-component vector stores signed amounts along three basis axes. In an orthonormal Cartesian frame the axes have unit length and are perpendicular. A displacement from point p to point q is q minus p. Adding a displacement to a point gives another point; subtracting two points gives a vector. Multiplying coordinates by a scale factor changes lengths, so metres and millimetres must not be mixed without conversion.

Alignment, not just distance

For unit vectors the dot product is the cosine itself: one means aligned, zero means perpendicular, and minus one means opposite. A cross product instead produces a perpendicular vector, whose direction depends on axis handedness and input order. A normalized vector divides each component by its length. That division is undefined for the zero vector, so software needs an explicit degeneracy rule instead of assuming every direction can be normalized.

Worked example

Take a=(3,4,0) and b=(-4,3,0). Both have length five. Their dot product is -12+12=0, so they are perpendicular. The unit direction of a is (0.6,0.8,0). These exact small values are useful fixtures: the answer can be checked without another graphics library.

Try it yourself

If every coordinate is multiplied by ten, what happens to length and squared distance?

Answer

Length grows by ten; squared distance grows by one hundred. Unit directions are unchanged for positive scaling. Negative scaling also reverses direction.

gffx boundary

Vectors are tensor data, not a separate new vector-class API. Existing transforms and normal operations consume them. A tensor's shape, dtype and device describe storage, not its physical units or coordinate frame. The caller must keep those meanings consistent. Read the linked operation fixtures for supported layouts; this introductory equation is not a new backend-support claim.
